html:
SMTO-SKL-0093 — Too many Microsoft sign-ins are still waiting to finish

GUID: 81feb118-6d5a-5dd5-9c5a-fb7154e38897
Slug: microsoft365-oauth-too-many-pending
Domain: SKL · Subsystem: microsoft365

What happened

  • Several Microsoft sign-in links were started and none have been finished yet. SMTO limits how many can wait at once, so it didn't start another one.

How to fix — simple steps

  1. If you still have a Microsoft sign-in tab open, finish signing in there. Finishing a waiting sign-in connects the account and frees up space.
  2. Otherwise, wait ten minutes without starting any new sign-ins. Each unfinished sign-in expires on its own after ten minutes.
  3. Then ask the Agent once to connect your Microsoft 365 account, and open only that newest link. One fresh request is all you need, and older links won't work after they expire.

What success looks like

  • The Agent gives you one sign-in link and the browser page says your account is connected.

If it still fails

  • If the error comes back right away, something may be starting sign-ins repeatedly. Select Copy error details and send them to the person who manages SMTO.

Technical details

Observed condition

  • BrowserOAuth.start refused a new Microsoft consent request because 32 unexpired pending authorization handshakes already exist (microsoft365.oauth_too_many_pending).

What this means

  • Shared browser OAuth already has the maximum supported number of live pending authorization transactions. This explanation performs no Microsoft request. The original operation stage and receipt determine its effect; keep the selected tenant, account and resource identity fixed during recovery.

Why this can happen

  • Shared browser OAuth already has the maximum supported number of live pending authorization transactions.

How to diagnose it

  • Inspect existing pending flows and their expiration instead of opening another one.

How to fix it

  • Complete the outstanding consent flows or let them expire (each handshake lives ten minutes in memory), then call microsoft365.connect once. Look for an Agent loop or script repeatedly calling connect.
  • Complete existing sign-in flows or allow them to expire before starting another connect request.

Retry and execution caution

  • Inspect provider state and exact account authority first.

How to verify the fix

  • Existing flows complete or expire before another consent request is admitted.

What not to do

  • Do not expose secrets or blindly replay uncertain mutations.

Technical notes

  • This explanation performs no Microsoft request. The original operation stage and receipt determine its effect; keep the selected tenant, account and resource identity fixed during recovery.
  • Preserve the occurrence ID and safe request/operation references. Receipts and occurrence facts establish what started or completed; the catalog does not authorize retries or establish execution outcome.
